title: Powers below one, roots in reverse gear, and counting the opposite
summary: Finish the exponent rules by walking the powers down past zero, meet the square root as the gear that undoes squaring, then count crowds two ways that feel like cheating: count what you do not want, and match the hard collection against an easy one.
materials: counters or coins to lay out pairs
a blank strip of paper for writing the powers of 2 in a row
two dice, one of each colour

problems.prompt: A drum pattern claps 40 times out of every 64 beats. What fraction of the beats are claps, in lowest terms?
explanation: Find the biggest number that divides both 40 and 64 evenly: that number is 8.
40 divided by 8 is 5, and 64 divided by 8 is 8.
So 40 out of 64 beats is 5/8 in lowest terms.
problems.useAgain: when a beat count has to be shrunk to its simplest fraction fast, and the common factor is bigger than 2.
hints: Both 40 and 64 share a common factor bigger than 2. Find the biggest one.
Divide the top and the bottom by that same factor in one move.
problems.socraticHint: Both 40 and 64 are even. Does dividing by 2 just once get you all the way to lowest terms here?

variant.prompt: A drum pattern claps 28 times out of every 70 beats. What fraction of the beats are claps, in lowest terms?

problems.prompt: A drum loop is 12 beats long and repeats. The band has to fill exactly 200 beats, so they play whole loops and then a short tail. How many beats long is the tail?
explanation: Keep only the leftover. The whole loops all look the same, so they are not what the question is asking about.
Count 12s toward 200. Sixteen loops make 192 beats.
Seventeen loops would need 204 beats, which is past the end.
200 take away 192 leaves a tail of eight beats.
problems.useAgain: when something repeats in equal blocks and you need what is left over at the end.
hints: Whole loops are all the same size, so find how many of them fit before you worry about the end.
Multiply 12 by whole numbers until you get as close to 200 as you can without passing it.
problems.socraticHint: If the band played one more whole loop, how far past 200 beats would that put them?

variant.prompt: A drum loop is 9 beats long and repeats. The band has to fill exactly 250 beats with whole loops and then a short tail. How many beats long is the tail?

problems.prompt: A cymbal crashes on every seventh beat: beat 7, beat 14, beat 21, and so on. How many crashes happen in the first 100 beats?
explanation: Count the steps before you count the beats. Each crash sits one 7 further along than the last.
Fourteen sevens make 98, which is still inside the first 100 beats.
Fifteen sevens would be 105, past the end, so that crash never happens.
That is count the steps first: work out how many times something happens before a limit, not by marching through every beat.
problems.useAgain: when you need how many times a repeating thing happens before a wall, not where it happens.
hints: The crashes are the multiples of 7. You want how many of them fit, not where the last one lands.
Divide 100 by 7 and look only at the whole part of the answer.
problems.socraticHint: Would a crash on beat 105 count? What does that tell you about where to stop?

variant.prompt: A cymbal crashes on every sixth beat: beat 6, beat 12, beat 18, and so on. How many crashes happen in the first 150 beats?

problems.prompt: A drum machine sits at 96 beats a minute. You double it twice, then halve it three times. What is it on now?
explanation: Doublings and halvings cancel each other off in pairs, so count them instead of chasing every number.
Two of the three halvings undo the two doublings. One halving is left over.
Half of 96 is 48.
problems.useAgain: when doublings and halvings are stacked and you can cancel them off in pairs.
hints: You do not have to work out every tempo. Count how many doublings and how many halvings there are.
A doubling followed by a halving leaves the tempo exactly where it started.
problems.socraticHint: If there had been three doublings and three halvings, where would the machine end up, and why?

variant.prompt: A drum machine sits at 120 beats a minute. You double it three times, then halve it four times. What is it on now?

problems.prompt: A drum machine starts a fade at 120 beats a minute and takes 12 beats a minute off the tempo at the end of every bar. It switches off as soon as the tempo is 40 or lower. How many bars does it play?
explanation: The tempo only falls, and always by the same 12, so it cannot dodge the wall at 40.
The 36 is the first tempo at 40 or lower, and it arrives at the end of the seventh bar.
A number that only falls toward a known wall has to stop, so this fade cannot run forever.
problems.useAgain: when something repeats and you need to know it must stop, not just that it probably does.
hints: Write the tempo at the end of each bar in a column, one under the other.
Take 12 off, look at the new tempo, and ask whether the machine is still allowed to play.
problems.socraticHint: The tempo never goes back up. What does that promise you about whether this fade ever ends?

variant.prompt: A drum machine starts a fade at 150 beats a minute and takes 20 off the tempo at the end of every bar. It switches off as soon as the tempo is 50 or lower. How many bars does it play?

problem.prompt: On graph paper draw a grid of streets with 4 corners across and 4 corners down, so it is 3 blocks each way. Start at the top left corner and walk to the bottom right corner, moving only right or down along the streets. How many different routes are there?
explanation: Do not draw routes. Label every corner with the number of routes that reach it.
Along the top row and down the left side there is only one way in, so write 1 on each of those corners.
Every other corner is entered from the corner above it or the corner to its left, and from nowhere else.
So its label is those two labels added. Fill the grid in row by row.
The bottom right corner comes out at 20, and you never drew a single route.
problem.useAgain: when routes are too many to draw and every place can be entered from only a few places.
hints: Trying to draw them all will lose you three of them. Label the corners instead.
A corner can only be entered from above or from the left. What does that say about its label?
problem.socraticHint: How many routes reach the corner one step right of the start, and why is that number so small?

variant.prompt: The same walk on a wider grid: 5 corners across and 3 corners down, which is 4 blocks across and 2 blocks down. Moving only right or down, how many different routes are there?

steps.title: Below the one, and back up the other way

problems.prompt: Write 2 to the power of negative 3 as a fraction.
explanation: Walk the powers of 2 downwards: 8, 4, 2, 1. Each step down halves the one before it.
Keep the same halving going past the 1: one half, one quarter, one eighth.
The step that lands on negative 3 is one eighth.
problems.useAgain: when a power is negative and you want it written as a plain fraction.
hints: Going down one power does the opposite of going up one power. What is the opposite of multiplying by 2?
Write the powers of 2 in a row and keep the pattern running past the 1.
problems.socraticHint: What has to sit at the power of zero for the halving pattern to stay unbroken?

variant.prompt: Write 3 to the power of negative 2 as a fraction.

problems.prompt:
Felix wrote 2 to the power of negative 4 as a fraction like this:
Line 1: Walk the powers of 2 downward: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Line 2: Keep the same halving going past the 1: one half, one quarter, one eighth.
Line 3: One more halving past one eighth gives one sixteenth.
Line 4: So 2 to the power of negative 4 equals 1/8.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 4 is wrong: line 3 already found the next halving to be 1/16, not 1/8.
Lines 1 to 3 are correct: the powers of 2 walk down as 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
The halving then reaches an eighth, then a sixteenth.
The slip stops one halving too early, copying an earlier value instead of the one line 3 just found.
The final answer has to match the last halving actually done, not an earlier one.
problems.useAgain: when you check a chain of halvings or thirdings for a negative exponent, since the final line has to match the last step actually taken.
hints: The halving chain shown here is correct up to a point; the trap is whether it goes far enough.
Walk the halving chain yourself, from 1 down through four halvings, and compare it with what the worked solution claims.
problems.socraticHint: The exponent is negative 4, meaning four halvings past 1. Does the worked solution's fraction match four halvings, or fewer?

variant.prompt:
Felix wrote 3 to the power of negative 3 as a fraction like this:
Line 1: Walk the powers of 3 downward: 27, 9, 3, 1.
Line 2: Keep the same thirding going past the 1: one third, one ninth, one twenty-seventh.
Line 3: So 3 to the power of negative 3 is 1/27, a fraction less than one.
Line 4: The negative sign on the exponent means the final answer must also be negative, so 3 to the power of negative 3 equals -1/27.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Simplify 7 squared divided by 7 to the fifth power, and write it as a fraction.
explanation: Write both sides out long: two 7s on top, five 7s underneath.
Cross off a 7 on top against a 7 underneath, twice. The top is used up and three 7s are left below.
Three 7s multiplied together make 343, so the answer is 1 over 343.
problems.useAgain: when the same base sits above and below a line and the bottom holds more of it.
hints: Do not reach for a rule. Write the 7s out long, on top and underneath.
Cross off one 7 from the top with one from the bottom and see what survives.
problems.socraticHint: Taking the powers away gives negative 3. Where does a negative power put the number, above the line or below it?

variant.prompt: Simplify 5 cubed divided by 5 to the sixth power, and write it as a fraction.

problems.prompt: A friend says that 5 to the power of negative 2 means minus 25. True or false?
explanation: A negative power is not a negative answer. The minus sign says which way along the pattern to walk.
Going down the powers of 5 divides by 5 each time: 125, 25, 5, 1.
Keeping that going gives one fifth, then one twenty fifth. The row never crosses zero.
problems.useAgain: when a rule about signs looks obvious and you want to test it against the pattern.
hints: Ask what the minus is doing. Is it changing the size of the number, or the direction of the pattern?
Write the powers of 5 in a row from 125 down through 1 and keep the pattern going.
problems.socraticHint: Every number in that row is positive. What would have to happen for the row to suddenly land below zero?

variant.prompt: Another friend says that 2 to the power of negative 1 is one half. True or false?

problems.prompt: What whole number multiplied by itself gives 196?
explanation: A square root is the reverse gear. Squaring asks what a number makes; the root asks what made this number.
10 times 10 is 100, too small. 15 times 15 is 225, too big.
So the number sits between those two. Trying the one just below 15 gives 196 exactly.
problems.useAgain: when a question hands you the square and wants the number that made it.
hints: Squaring and rooting are one gearbox in two directions. What could be squared to land on 196?
Try 10 and try 15 first. Does the number you want sit between them or outside them?
problems.socraticHint: The square ends in a 6. Which digits, squared, can leave a 6 at the end?

variant.prompt: What whole number multiplied by itself gives 289?

problems.prompt: The square root of 60 sits between which two whole numbers?
explanation: Squares are far easier to test than roots, so square the candidates instead of rooting the 60.
7 times 7 is 49, which is under 60. 8 times 8 is 64, which is over it.
60 is caught between 49 and 64, so its root is caught between 7 and 8.
problems.useAgain: when a root is not a whole number and you only need the two whole numbers it lives between.
hints: You never need the root itself. Find two square numbers with 60 sitting between them.
Say the square numbers out loud: 36, 49, 64, 81. Where does 60 land?
problems.socraticHint: Is 60 nearer to 49 or to 64, and what does that say about which end the root leans toward?

variant.prompt: The square root of 90 sits between which two whole numbers?

problems.prompt: A square vegetable patch covers 324 square feet. How many feet of edging goes all the way around it?
explanation: A square's area is one side multiplied by itself, so the side is the square root of the area.
18 times 18 is 324, so each side is 18 feet.
Going all the way around is four of those sides: 18 multiplied by 4 is the length of edging.
problems.useAgain: when a square's area is given and the question is really about its side.
hints: The area is not the answer and it is not the side either. Find the side first.
What number multiplied by itself makes 324? Start at 20 and come down.
problems.socraticHint: If the patch had four times the area, would it need four times the edging?

variant.prompt: A square vegetable patch covers 400 square feet. How many feet of edging goes all the way around it?

steps.title: The diagonal you can trust, and tickets weighed against the cost

problems.prompt: A rectangular shop shelf is 12 cm tall and 16 cm wide. What is the length of its diagonal, in cm?
explanation: The shelf's diagonal is the longest side of a right triangle whose legs are the height and width.
12 squared plus 16 squared is 144 plus 256, which is 400.
The square root of 400 is 20 cm.
problems.useAgain: when a rectangle's diagonal is needed and its two edges give you a right triangle's two legs.
hints: The diagonal is the longest side of a right triangle made from the height and width. Square both legs and add.
Take the square root of that sum to get the diagonal.
problems.socraticHint: If you square both edges of the shelf and add them, what does the square root of that total give you?

variant.prompt: A rectangular shop shelf is 9 cm tall and 12 cm wide. What is the length of its diagonal, in cm?

problems.prompt: A 13 m ladder leans against a wall, reaching 12 m up the wall. How far is the base of the ladder from the wall, in m?
explanation: The ladder is the longest side of a right triangle; the wall height and the ground distance are the two legs.
13 squared minus 12 squared is 169 minus 144, which is 25.
The square root of 25 is 5 m.
problems.useAgain: when the longest side and one leg of a right triangle are known and the other leg is missing.
hints: The ladder is the longest side of the triangle. Which two numbers are the two legs and the longest side here?
Subtract the known leg's square from the ladder's square, then take the square root.
problems.socraticHint: If you already know the longest side and one leg, do you add or subtract the two squares to find the missing leg?

variant.prompt: A 10 m ladder leans against a wall, reaching 8 m up the wall. How far is the base of the ladder from the wall, in m?

problems.prompt: Game A costs 2 tickets to play, and wins 5 tickets half the time, otherwise 0. Game B costs 2 tickets and always wins 2 tickets. Which game has the higher expected value?
explanation: Game A's expected value is 5 times 1/2, plus 0 times 1/2, which is 2.5 tickets.
Game B's expected value is always exactly 2 tickets, since it never varies.
2.5 is more than 2, so Game A has the higher expected value.
problems.useAgain: when two games' expected values need comparing, not just their costs or their biggest possible prize.
hints: Work out each game's expected value on its own before comparing.
A game that always pays the same amount has that amount as its expected value.
problems.socraticHint: Does a bigger possible prize always mean a bigger expected value, once you weigh it by how often it happens?

variant.prompt: Game A costs 2 tickets and wins 6 tickets a third of the time, otherwise 0. Game B costs 2 tickets and always wins 3 tickets. Which game has the higher expected value?

problems.prompt: A game costs 3 tickets to play. It pays 9 tickets a third of the time, otherwise 0. Is the game fair, better than fair, or worse than fair for the player?
options: Fair: the expected payout equals the cost
Better than fair for the player
Worse than fair for the player
explanation: The expected payout is 9 times 1/3, which is 3 tickets.
3 tickets expected is exactly equal to the 3 ticket cost.
Equal payout and cost makes this game fair.
problems.useAgain: when a game's cost and expected payout need comparing to decide fair, better, or worse than fair.
hints: Multiply the possible payout by its chance to get the expected value.
Compare that number directly to the cost.
problems.socraticHint: If the expected payout comes out exactly equal to the cost, is there any long-run edge for either side?

variant.prompt: A game costs 3 tickets to play. It pays 10 tickets a quarter of the time, otherwise 0. Is the game fair, better than fair, or worse than fair for the player?
options: Fair: the expected payout equals the cost
Better than fair for the player
Worse than fair for the player

figure.alt: White to move. A white knight on c4 can capture a black pawn on e5, forking a black queen on d7 and a black rook on f7.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move captures a pawn and attacks two pieces at once?
explanation: Nxe5 takes a free pawn and lands on a square that attacks both d7 and f7.
Black's queen and rook sit on exactly those two squares.
White wins a pawn now and more material next move.
problems.useAgain: when a capture also lands your piece on a square that forks two others.
hints: Before you capture, check what the knight would attack from its new square.
Look at both of the two squares it would attack from there.
problems.socraticHint: Does this move only win a pawn, or does it threaten something bigger too?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move captures a pawn and attacks two pieces at once?

figure.alt: White to move. A white knight on g3 can capture a black pawn on f5, forking a black rook on d6 and a black queen on h6.
White to move. A white bishop on f1 faces a black knight on d5, with the black king on g8 on the same diagonal.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move pins the black knight to its king?
explanation: Black's king on g8 and knight on d5 share the same long diagonal.
Bc4 lines the bishop up on that diagonal, right behind the knight.
The knight cannot step off that diagonal without leaving its king in check.
problems.useAgain: when an enemy piece and its king share a diagonal your bishop can reach.
hints: Which diagonal already holds both the black king and the black knight?
Move your bishop onto that same diagonal, behind the knight.
problems.socraticHint: What does the knight shield its own king from right now?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move pins the black knight to its king?

figure.alt: White to move. A white bishop on h5 faces a black knight on e4, with the black king on a8 on the same diagonal.
White to move. Black's king on h8 has pawns on g7 and h7, a white king stands on f8, and a white knight on h6 can jump in.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?
explanation: Black's king on h8 has pawns on g7 and h7, leaving only g8 open.
Your own king on f8 already covers g8.
Nf7 checks the king with every square covered, so it is mate.
problems.useAgain: when your own king covers the one square a knight check would otherwise leave open.
hints: The king's own pawns leave one square open. Does anything else cover it?
Find the knight move that checks the king directly.
problems.socraticHint: Could the black king step toward the corner to escape this check?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?

figure.alt: White to move. Black's king on a8 has pawns on a7 and b7, a white king stands on c8, and a white knight on a6 can jump in.
Black to move. Black's king sits on h8 with a pawn on a7, boxed in by a white king on f6 and a white queen on f7.

problems.prompt: It is black's move. The king has no square to go to. Is this checkmate, stalemate, or does black have another legal move?
explanation: The black king on h8 truly cannot move anywhere.
But the black pawn on a7 can still push forward.
One legal move anywhere on the board means the game is not over.
problems.useAgain: when a king looks stuck, so check every other piece before calling it a stalemate.
hints: Do not only check the king. Does any other black piece have a move?
Look at the far side of the board for a piece that has not moved yet.
problems.socraticHint: Does stalemate mean the king has no move, or that the whole side has no move?

variant.prompt: It is black's move. The king has no square to go to. Is this checkmate, stalemate, or does black have another legal move?

figure.alt: Black to move. Black's king sits on a8 with a pawn on h7, boxed in by a white king on c5 and a white queen on b6.

steps.title: Counting without counting: the opposite, and the match

problems.prompt: How many of the whole numbers from 1 to 200 are not multiples of 4?
explanation: Counting the ones you do not want is often the smaller job, so count the multiples of 4 instead.
Every fourth number is a multiple of 4, and 200 divided by 4 is 50, so there are 50 of them.
Every number from 1 to 200 is either a multiple of 4 or not, never both.
So take the 50 off the 200, and the rest are the numbers you were asked for.
problems.useAgain: when the things you want are many and the things you do not want are few.
hints: Listing every number that is not a multiple of 4 would take all morning. What is the short list?
How many multiples of 4 are there up to 200? That is a division, not a list.
problems.socraticHint: Every number here lands in exactly one of two piles. Once you know one pile, what work is left?

variant.prompt: How many of the whole numbers from 1 to 300 are not multiples of 6?

problems.prompt: Two dice are rolled, a red one and a blue one, giving 36 possible outcomes. In how many of them does at least one die show a 6?
explanation: At least one is a warning sign. Counting the red sixes and the blue sixes and adding them counts one roll twice.
Count the opposite instead: neither die shows a 6, so each die has 5 faces left.
5 times 5 is 25 outcomes with no 6 anywhere.
Take those off the 36 and what remains has at least one 6 in it.
problems.useAgain: when a question says at least one and counting it head on counts something twice.
hints: Adding the red sixes to the blue sixes counts one particular roll twice. Which roll?
Count the rolls with no 6 on either die first, then take them off the 36.
problems.socraticHint: How many faces are left on one die once the 6 is forbidden?

variant.prompt: Two dice are rolled, a red one and a blue one, giving 36 possible outcomes. In how many of them does at least one die show an odd number?

problems.prompt: Eight cows meet at the gate and every cow touches noses with every other cow exactly once. How many nose touches happen?
explanation: Stand with one cow. She has to greet the other seven.
That is true of all eight cows, which gives 8 times 7, or 56 greetings.
But every touch has two cows in it, so it was counted from both ends.
Halving 56 undoes the double count.
problems.useAgain: when everyone in a group meets everyone else and each meeting has two ends.
hints: Start with one cow. How many other cows does she have to greet?
Do that for every cow, then look hard at whether any greeting got counted more than once.
problems.socraticHint: When the brown cow greets the spotted cow, whose count does that touch land in?

variant.prompt: Twelve cows meet at the gate and every cow touches noses with every other cow exactly once. How many nose touches happen?

problems.prompt: A stop sign has 8 corners. Straight lines are drawn joining every pair of corners. Eight of those lines are the sides of the sign. How many of the lines are diagonals?
explanation: A line is nothing but a choice of two corners, so count the pairs of corners.
Each corner pairs with the other seven: 8 times 7 is 56, and every pair was counted from both ends.
Half of 56 is 28 lines altogether.
The eight sides are lines too, and they are not diagonals, so take them off the 28.
problems.useAgain: when a shape's diagonals are wanted and the sides have to come back out of the count.
hints: Every line is decided by the two corners it joins. Count those choices first.
Count all the lines the pairing gives you, then ask which of them nobody would call a diagonal.
problems.socraticHint: Why do the sides turn up in the pair count at all, when a side is not a diagonal?

variant.prompt: A hexagon has 6 corners, and straight lines join every pair of them. Six of those lines are the sides. How many are diagonals?

problems.prompt: A milkshake stand has 4 different toppings. Each topping is either on your milkshake or not on it. How many different milkshakes can be ordered, counting the plain one with nothing on it?
explanation: Match each milkshake with a row of four answers, yes or no for each topping, always in the same order.
Every milkshake gives one row and every row gives one milkshake, so counting rows counts milkshakes.
Each of the four answers has 2 ways to go, so the rows number 2 times 2 times 2 times 2.
The row of four noes is the plain milkshake, which is why it belongs in the count.
problems.useAgain: when a thing is hard to count and each one can be matched with something easy to count.
hints: Forget the milkshakes for a moment. What does one topping decide, and how many ways can it be decided?
Write a yes or a no for each of the four toppings, and count how many different lines you could write.
problems.socraticHint: Could two different milkshakes ever be written as the same row of yeses and noes?

variant.prompt: A milkshake stand has 5 different toppings, each either on or off. How many different milkshakes can be ordered, counting the plain one?

problems.prompt: A row of 6 lamps stands on a shelf. Each lamp is either on or off. How many different pictures can the row show?
explanation: Match each picture with a binary number six digits long, writing 1 for on and 0 for off.
Every picture is one such binary number, and every such binary number is one picture.
So the two collections have exactly the same size, and the binary one is easy to count.
Six digit binary runs from 000000 to 111111, which is 0 up to 63 in ordinary numbers.
A list that starts counting at 0 holds one more than its last number.
problems.useAgain: when two collections can be paired one for one, so counting the easy one counts the hard one.
hints: You already know a way of writing on and off with digits. Use it on the whole row at once.
How many binary numbers are six digits long, if a leading zero is allowed?
problems.socraticHint: Why does the row with nothing switched on still count as a picture?

variant.prompt: A row of 8 lamps stands on a shelf, each one either on or off. How many different pictures can the row show?

problems.prompt: A counting peak in the AMC 8 style, untimed, and you explain it back afterwards. How many three digit numbers contain at least one digit 7?
explanation: Head on, a 7 could sit in any of three places at once, and the overlaps make a mess.
Count the opposite: three digit numbers with no 7 anywhere.
The first digit has 8 ways, since 0 and 7 are both barred. The other two digits have 9 ways each.
8 times 9 times 9 is 648 numbers with no 7 in them.
There are 900 three digit numbers in all, so take the 648 away from the 900.
problems.useAgain: when at least one is asked across several places and the overlaps make a direct count a mess.
hints: A number can hold two or three 7s, so adding up the places counts some numbers more than once.
Count the three digit numbers with no 7 at all, and watch the first digit, which cannot be 0 either.
problems.socraticHint: How many digits are still allowed in the hundreds place once the 7 is banned?

variant.prompt: How many three digit numbers contain at least one digit 0?

problems.prompt: A second peak, untimed. Two different numbers are chosen from 1 to 10. In how many ways can they be chosen so that they add up to an even number?
explanation: A sum is even only when both numbers are odd or both are even. One of each always gives an odd sum.
There are 5 odd numbers here. Counting from each one gives 5 times 4, and every pair got counted from both ends, so halve it.
That is 10 pairs of odd numbers, and the 5 even numbers give another 10 the same way.
Add the two cases together.
problems.useAgain: when pairs are counted inside separate cases and each pair still has two ends.
hints: When is a sum of two numbers even? Try a few pairs before you count anything.
Split into the both odd case and the both even case, and count the pairs inside each.
problems.socraticHint: Does the pair 3 and 5 get counted once or twice when you count outwards from each number in turn?

variant.prompt: Two different numbers are chosen from 1 to 12. In how many ways can they be chosen so that they add up to an even number?

steps.title: Explain it in writing: why a matching counts both sides
steps.prompt: Write the milkshake count as an argument, not as a total you happened to reach. Say what you matched each milkshake with, then say the two things that make a matching honest: no two milkshakes share a row, and no row is left without a milkshake. Then do the lamps the same way. Finish that part by saying what a stand with 6 toppings would have to come to, and why it has to land on exactly the same number as the 6 lamps, even though one is a shelf and one is a drink. Finish with the one sentence a matching earns you: if two collections can be paired off one for one, counting either one counts both.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Record the three digit number count out loud, with your working on paper in shot. Start by saying what goes wrong if you count the numbers with a 7 directly, and give an example of a number that would get counted twice. Then count the opposite out loud, one digit place at a time, saying why the hundreds place has fewer choices than the other two. Finish by looking at the camera and saying how you know the two piles together make every three digit number, with none left over and none in both.
